title: Basic Structure Doctrine & SC Bench Precedents
subtitle: Evolution of Constitutional Amendment Boundaries (Art. 368 vs. Art. 13)
summary: Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution, but the Supreme Court established that Parliament cannot alter or destroy the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Constitution.

keyMilestones.case: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
keyMilestones.ruling: SC ruled Parliament can amend ANY part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
SC reversed earlier view: Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be abridged by Constitutional amendments.

keyMilestones.case: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
keyMilestones.ruling: 13-Judge Bench (Largest in SC history) delivered 7:6 majority verdict. Introduced 'Basic Structure Doctrine'. Parliament CAN amend Constitutional provisions EXCEPT its basic structure.

keyMilestones.case: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
keyMilestones.ruling: Reaffirmed Basic Structure. Stated that judicial review and harmony between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and DPSPs (Part IV) are part of the basic structure.

keyArticles.desc: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor.
Appointment of Supreme Court Judges by the President by warrant under hand and seal.
Appointment of High Court Judges.
Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Presidential Reference).

examTraps: Trap: Don't confuse Golaknath (1967) with Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Golaknath barred altering FRs; Kesavananda allowed amending FRs as long as basic structure is preserved.
Trap: 'Basic Structure' is NOT explicitly defined in the text of the Constitution of India—it is a judicially evolved doctrine.
memoryTip: Mnemonic: S-G-K-M (Shankari 1951 -> Golaknath 1967 -> Kesavananda 1973 -> Minerva 1980). Bench size in Kesavananda = 13 Judges.

title: Supreme Court Pendency
subtitle: The conclusion of the Supreme Court's Samadhan Samaroh Special Lok Adalat connects judicial pendency and access to justice with the Legal Services Authorities Act, consent-based settlement, the legal effect of Lok Adalat awards, and the distinction between regular and Permanent Lok Adalats.
summary:
The Supreme Court concluded **Samadhan Samaroh 2026** with a three-day Special Lok Adalat held on 21, 22 and 23 August 2026. The name expands to **Supreme Court Action for Mediated Adjudication and Disputes Harmonization Across Nation**. The initiative had begun on 21 April with pre-settlement work through legal-services institutions and mediation centres; its stated purpose was amicable resolution of suitable matters pending before the Supreme Court through consent-based processes.

The Supreme Court's consolidated statement, released on 24 August, reported **3,285 matters listed**, **1,664 matters settled or disposed of through Lok Adalat**, and **48 matters resolved through mediation**—a total of **1,712 resolved matters**. It also reported disbursements of **₹2,40,94,37,087.38** (about ₹240.94 crore). The day-wise Lok Adalat figures were 402 disposals out of 588 listed on 21 August, 350 out of 1,159 on 22 August, and 912 out of 1,538 on 23 August. These consolidated figures supersede the interim counts reported while the exercise was still under way.

keyMilestones.event: The Forty-second Constitutional Amendment inserts Article 39A on equal justice and free legal aid.
Parliament enacts the Legal Services Authorities Act.
The Act comes into force; 9 November is observed as National Legal Services Day.
Chapter VI-A introduces Permanent Lok Adalats for specified public utility services.
The Supreme Court holds a Special Lok Adalat during its 75th anniversary year.
Samadhan Samaroh begins its pre-settlement phase.
Sixteen Supreme Court Special Lok Adalat benches list more than 600 matters on day one; more than 400 settlements are reported.
The three-day Special Lok Adalat and Samadhan Samaroh culmination phase conclude.
The Supreme Court releases consolidated results: 3,285 matters listed; 1,664 Lok Adalat disposals; 48 mediated resolutions; 1,712 total; and about ₹240.94 crore disbursed.

keyArticles.desc: Article 39A: Equal justice and free legal aid.
Legal Services Authorities Act: Enacted in 1987 and brought into force on 9 November 1995.
National Legal Services Day: Observed on 9 November.
NALSA patron-in-chief: The Chief Justice of India; its executive chairman is a serving or retired Supreme Court judge nominated in accordance with the Act.
Lok Adalat meaning: Commonly translated as “People's Court.”
Regular Lok Adalat award: Deemed civil-court decree/order, final and binding, with no ordinary appeal.
Permanent Lok Adalat: A distinct statutory body for specified public utility services.
Supreme Court seat: New Delhi under Article 130, subject to the constitutional mechanism for sitting elsewhere.

title: Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure
subtitle: SEBI's IT Resilience Index and FIRE-aligned incident reporting turn cyber resilience into a measurable regulatory obligation for core securities-market infrastructure, linking statutory regulation, operational continuity and internationally harmonised incident reporting.
summary:
On **24 August 2026**, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) issued two connected cyber-resilience circulars. The first creates a **100-point IT Resilience Index (ITRI)** for all stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories except AMC Repo Clearing Limited. The index is intended to provide an early-warning and supervisory measure of whether critical securities-market infrastructure can maintain continuous service.

The second aligns SEBI's Cyber Incident Reporting Portal with the Financial Stability Board's **Format for Incident Reporting Exchange (FIRE)**. SEBI-regulated entities retain the existing initial timelines—email within six hours and portal reporting within 24 hours—but will use common fields, definitions, classifications and staged lifecycle updates. SEBI also launched the **Cyber Suraksha Portal**, a separate knowledge hub for circulars, vulnerability warnings and incident insights; it is not the incident-reporting portal.

The Industry Standards Forum is to finalise detailed ITRI scoring criteria.
MIIs are to finalise their ITRI standard operating procedure.
MIIs must operationalise the ITRI.
First reporting period; the score is due within 60 days.

CERT-In: National incident-response agency under Section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

title: BRICS Developments
subtitle: The Jaipur, Chennai and Visakhapatnam sectoral declarations are consecutive outcomes of India's 2026 BRICS chairship, linking consensus diplomacy with tourism, frontier technology, sports governance and the distinction between political commitments and binding law.
summary:
BRICS Tourism Ministers adopted the **Jaipur Declaration** by consensus at their ministerial meeting in Jaipur on 21 August 2026. The declaration identifies four priorities: use of artificial intelligence in tourism; sustainable and responsible tourism; skilling and capacity-building; and greater exchanges and seamless travel among BRICS countries.

The meeting used the theme **“Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”** Ministers also identified cooperation in destination management, tourism data and statistics, investment and infrastructure, heritage, and people-to-people contact. Representatives of nine BRICS members participated.

On 22 August, the 14th BRICS Science, Technology and Innovation Ministerial Meeting in Chennai unanimously adopted the **Chennai Declaration**. It endorsed an effective, resilient and future-ready STI framework; the 2026-27 STI calendar; work on research infrastructure and mega-science; and further operationalisation of the **BRICS Global Research Advanced Infrastructure Network (BRICS GRAIN)**. Cooperation areas include AI, high-performance computing, quantum technologies, biotechnology, health, advanced materials and climate-related research.

On 23 August, BRICS Sports Ministers adopted the **BRICS Sports Joint Declaration** by consensus at Visakhapatnam. They advanced three practical initiatives: a BRICS Working Group on Sports Technology; a proposed BRICS Sports Manufacturing Conclave in Udaipur in November 2026; and proposed Traditional and Indigenous Sports Demonstration Games in Ahmedabad on 12-13 October 2026. The working group covers sports science, athlete performance, governance, artificial intelligence, digital transformation and innovation. The Jaipur, Chennai and Visakhapatnam texts are ministerial political commitments and cooperation frameworks; none was presented as a ratified treaty creating enforceable individual rights.

title: European Union Artificial Intelligence Act
subtitle: The EU AI Act joins technology regulation, fundamental rights, extraterritorial jurisdiction, risk classification, deepfake transparency, institutional enforcement, and the distinction between an EU regulation and a directive.
summary: On 2 August 2026, the main application milestone under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act arrived. Transparency duties under Article 50 became applicable, including duties to tell people when they are interacting directly with certain AI systems and to make AI-generated or manipulated content identifiable in specified circumstances. The European Commission's AI Office also obtained enforcement powers over general-purpose AI models. This did not make every high-risk-system obligation immediately applicable: a 2026 amending measure postponed major high-risk rules to later dates.

keyMilestones.event: The European Parliament and Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act.
The Regulation entered into force, twenty days after publication in the Official Journal.
Rules on prohibited AI practices, definitions, and AI literacy began to apply.
Governance provisions and obligations for general-purpose AI models began to apply.
The Digital Omnibus amending Regulation entered into force and revised the high-risk implementation timetable.
Article 50 transparency duties became applicable and the AI Office obtained enforcement powers concerning general-purpose AI models.
The revised date for major obligations concerning high-risk systems listed in Annex III.
The revised date for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products listed in Annex I.

keyArticles.desc: Risk-based regulation governs Legal duties intensify with the potential harm of an AI use, ranging from prohibited practices to high-risk controls and transparency requirements.

Fundamental-rights protection governs The framework addresses equality, privacy, data protection, dignity, freedom of expression, effective remedy, and democratic integrity in contexts such as biometric identification, employment, education, policing, and access to essential services.

Article 50 transparency governs Covered providers must inform people when they interact directly with AI, while specified AI-generated or manipulated content must be marked or disclosed; deployers also have duties for deepfakes and certain public-interest content.
Extraterritorial reach governs A provider established outside the EU can still fall within scope when it places covered technology on the EU market or when the system's output is used in the EU.

Enforcement and proportionality governs National authorities and the AI Office divide enforcement responsibility. The Act provides tiered administrative fines, with the highest statutory ceiling for certain prohibited practices reaching the greater of €35 million or 7 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, subject to the applicable legal conditions.
EU regulation versus directive: A regulation is binding in its entirety and directly applicable; a directive binds member states as to the result but normally requires national implementation.
EU membership: The European Union has 27 member states and is distinct from the 46-member Council of Europe.
General-purpose AI model: A model capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks, which may be integrated into many downstream systems.
Deepfake: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content resembling real persons, objects, places, entities, or events and appearing authentic or truthful.
Risk tiers: Prohibited practices, high-risk systems, transparency-risk uses, and lower-risk uses do not carry identical legal duties.
Brussels effect: Large-market regulation may influence business conduct and technical standards beyond the regulator's territory.

examTraps: Do not say the AI Act entered into force on 2 August 2026; it entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies through a phased timetable.
Do not equate the European Union with the Council of Europe, or assume that a regulation and a directive operate identically.
memoryTip: “24 force, 26 disclose, 27–28 high risk”—entry into force in 2024, transparency in 2026, and revised high-risk dates in 2027 and 2028.

title: United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation
subtitle: The negotiations connect treaty-making, fiscal sovereignty, allocation of cross-border taxing rights, digital services, dispute resolution, development finance, UN voting, and India's constitutional rules on taxation and treaty implementation.
summary: On 3 August 2026, the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee opened its fifth substantive session at United Nations Headquarters in New York. The session runs through 13 August. For the first time in this process, member states are expected to negotiate concrete draft language across three linked workstreams: a United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, an early protocol on taxing income from cross-border services, and an early protocol on preventing and resolving tax disputes. This is a negotiating milestone, not the adoption or entry into force of a treaty. The committee is working toward final texts for consideration by the UN General Assembly in 2027.

keyMilestones.event: The UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 78/230, beginning the formal process for a UN framework convention on international tax cooperation.
General Assembly Resolution 79/235 adopted the terms of reference and established the intergovernmental negotiating committee.
The committee held its organizational session at UN Headquarters in New York.
The first substantive negotiating session began in New York.
The fourth substantive session concluded after work on the convention and the two early protocols.
The fifth session opened in New York, moving the process from concepts toward negotiation of concrete draft legal language.

keyArticles.desc: Article 265 of the Constitution governs No tax may be levied or collected in India except by authority of law; an international negotiation cannot itself impose a domestic tax.
Article 253 of the Constitution governs Parliament may make laws for implementing treaties, agreements, conventions, and decisions made at international conferences.
Article 51(c) of the Constitution governs The State should foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; it is a Directive Principle, not an independent charging provision for tax.
Union List, Entry 82 governs Parliament has legislative competence over taxes on income other than agricultural income.

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 governs It enables the Central Government to enter into and notify agreements with foreign countries or specified territories on double-tax relief, avoidance, information exchange, and recovery of tax.

Fiscal sovereignty and coordination governs Source countries, residence countries, and market jurisdictions may assert competing claims over the same cross-border income, creating risks of both double taxation and non-taxation.

Dispute resolution and due process governs The second early protocol may shape how cross-border tax disputes are prevented and resolved, raising questions of transparency, consistency, taxpayer protection, and state consent.
Framework convention: A treaty structure that sets broad principles, institutions, and procedures, often supplemented by more detailed protocols.
Protocol: A related legal instrument that can add detailed rules or obligations to a wider treaty framework.
Source jurisdiction: The country claiming taxing rights because income arises from activity, assets, customers, or payments connected with its territory.
Residence jurisdiction: The country claiming taxing rights because the taxpayer is resident there.
Permanent establishment: A treaty concept commonly used to decide when an enterprise has sufficient presence in another state for that state to tax specified business profits.
Double taxation: The same income may be taxed by more than one jurisdiction; treaties can allocate taxing rights and provide relief.
Base erosion and profit shifting: Arrangements that exploit gaps or mismatches in tax rules to shift profits away from the place of economic activity.

UN General Assembly: The principal deliberative organ of the UN, composed of all 193 member states; its resolutions do not by themselves convert a draft convention into a binding treaty for every state.

examTraps: Do not describe the current drafts as a binding treaty or say the UN has imposed a worldwide tax.
Do not confuse the UN framework-convention process with the separate OECD/G20 international tax process.
Do not treat a framework convention and its protocols as identical instruments, or treaty negotiation and Indian domestic implementation as the same legal stage.
memoryTip: “Framework, services, disputes—text in 26, target in 27.”

category: desertification, land degradation, drought, rangelands and pastoralism
title: UNCCD COP17 and India’s Open Natural Ecosystems Guide
subtitle: COP17 connects a legally binding Rio Convention, treaty institutions, drought governance, SDG 15.3, land-degradation neutrality, the 2026 International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, and India’s first guide to grasslands and other open natural ecosystems.
summary:
The seventeenth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) opened in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, on 17 August 2026. The conference is scheduled to continue until 28 August under the theme “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.” Its agenda covers land restoration, drought resilience, rangelands, pastoralists, food systems, finance and the implementation of the Convention.

On the opening day, India launched its first **Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems of India** at an official COP17 side event. The Guide covers grasslands, savannas, deserts, scrublands, rocky plateaus, ravines and related open landscapes, together with their biodiversity, ecological functions and connections to pastoral and other livelihoods. It is a scientific and policy resource, not a new statute or treaty amendment. COP17’s final negotiated decisions were still pending at the verification cut-off; the completed developments recorded here are the opening of the conference and the publication of India’s Guide.

keyMilestones.event: The United Nations Conference on Desertification was held in Nairobi and placed desertification on the international agenda.

The Rio Earth Summit recommended negotiation of a convention to combat desertification; the UNCCD became one of the three Rio Conventions alongside the UNFCCC and the Convention on Biological Diversity.
The UNCCD was adopted in Paris.
India deposited its instrument of ratification.
The Convention entered into force internationally.
The Convention entered into force for India.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals included Target 15.3, which calls for combating desertification, restoring degraded land and soil, and striving for a land-degradation-neutral world by 2030.
The UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 76/253 without a vote, declaring 2026 the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists.
UNCCD COP16 met in Riyadh; Parties adopted decisions on drought, land tenure, rangelands and pastoralists but left further work on a global drought instrument for the next cycle.
COP17 opened in Ulaanbaatar, and India launched its first Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems.
Scheduled closing date for COP17; final decisions must be verified separately after adoption.

keyArticles.desc: Legally binding Convention governs The UNCCD binds its Parties under international law. Article 2 focuses on combating desertification and mitigating drought through integrated, long-term strategies and international cooperation.

General obligations governs Article 4 calls for integrated approaches, international cooperation and coordination of financial and institutional mechanisms. More detailed implementation also occurs through national programmes and COP decisions.

COP decisions versus treaty amendments governs A COP decision may guide implementation under the Convention, but it is not automatically a textual amendment to the treaty. Draft language, agenda items and side-event publications are not adopted COP outcomes.

Drought-instrument question governs COP17 draft text contains bracketed alternatives concerning a possible global framework or protocol and whether a future instrument should be legally binding. No settled legal form existed at the cut-off.

keyArticles.article: Article 253 of the Constitution of India
keyArticles.desc: Article 253 of the Constitution of India governs Parliament may make laws to implement treaties, international agreements and decisions made at international conferences. Treaty participation does not by itself answer which domestic measure is required in every case.
Article 48A governs This Directive Principle directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
Article 51A(g) governs Citizens have a fundamental duty to protect and improve the natural environment and to have compassion for living creatures.

Status of India’s Guide governs The Guide is a scientific and policy resource. It does not itself amend the Environment (Protection) Act, change land title, create a protected area, or impose a directly enforceable prohibition.
Three Rio Conventions: The UNCCD, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) emerged from the 1992 Rio process.
Parties: The UNCCD has 197 Parties—196 country Parties plus the European Union.
Headquarters: The UNCCD Secretariat is in Bonn, Germany.
COP17 host and theme: Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia; “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.”
Land-degradation neutrality: SDG Target 15.3 seeks a world in which the amount and quality of land resources needed to support ecosystems and food security remain stable or increase by 2030.

Open Natural Ecosystems: Naturally open landscapes include grasslands, savannas, deserts, scrublands, rocky plateaus and ravines. Absence of dense tree cover does not by itself make them degraded land.
Rangelands and pastoralism: Rangelands support grazing and mobile or semi-mobile livestock systems; pastoral communities may depend on seasonal access and ecological knowledge.
International Year: UN General Assembly Resolution 76/253 declared 2026 the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists.

examTraps: Do not call every open landscape degraded or equate the UNCCD with the UNFCCC.
Do not treat a draft as an adopted COP decision or describe India’s Guide as a binding statute.
memoryTip: “Land, drought, livelihoods—17 in Ulaanbaatar; 15.3 for neutrality.”

category: Indo-Pacific, maritime security, defence technology and the Quad
title: India–Japan Maritime Security Cooperation
subtitle: The new maritime cooperation arrangement connects India–Japan relations, the Quad, freedom of navigation, joint naval capability, executive agreements and the rules-based Indo-Pacific.
summary:
On 20 August 2026, Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi met in New Delhi and signed a **Memorandum of Arrangement on Maritime Security Cooperation**. Their joint statement called for deeper defence cooperation in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific.

The two sides identified naval visits and exercises, training and personnel exchanges, logistics, maritime-domain cooperation and defence equipment and technology as fields for implementation. They also agreed to explore cooperation in naval shipbuilding and design by combining Japanese technology with Indian production capability. The arrangement strengthens an existing partnership; it is not a mutual-defence treaty, a military alliance or a declaration of war against any third country.

keyMilestones.event: India and Japan established diplomatic relations through a bilateral peace treaty.
The relationship became a Global Partnership.
It was upgraded to a Strategic and Global Partnership.
The countries issued their Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation.
The first bilateral Japan–India Maritime Exercise, JIMEX, was held.
The partnership was upgraded to a Special Strategic and Global Partnership.
The countries signed and brought into force their Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement for reciprocal logistics support.
India and Japan issued an updated Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation.
Their annual summit advanced defence technology, economic security and maritime cooperation.
The defence ministers signed the Memorandum of Arrangement on Maritime Security Cooperation in New Delhi.

keyArticles.desc: Executive arrangement governs A Memorandum of Arrangement records agreed cooperation between governments. Its legal effect depends on its language and domestic law; it should not automatically be described as a ratified treaty or parliamentary statute.
Article 73 governs The Union’s executive power generally extends to matters on which Parliament can legislate, including defence and foreign affairs.
Article 253 governs Parliament may legislate to implement treaties, international agreements and decisions made at international conferences.
Union List governs Defence, armed forces, foreign affairs and diplomatic relations fall within Union competence.
UNCLOS governs Both countries support navigation and a rules-based maritime order, subject to rights and duties under the law of the sea.
No collective-defence clause established governs The arrangement does not create a NATO-style obligation that an attack on one is an attack on the other.
Quad status governs The Quad is not founded on a collective-defence treaty and has no supranational legislature or permanent military command.
Quad members: India, Japan, Australia and the United States.
JIMEX: Bilateral maritime exercise between the Indian Navy and Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force.
Malabar: Naval exercise involving the four Quad countries; it began as an India–US exercise.
Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean: The term Indo-Pacific links two connected maritime theatres through crucial sea lanes.
UNCLOS: Adopted in 1982 and in force from 1994; it sets rules for territorial seas, exclusive economic zones and the high seas.
Territorial sea: Generally extends up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline.
Exclusive Economic Zone: Generally extends up to 200 nautical miles, subject to UNCLOS rules.

examTraps: A Memorandum of Arrangement is not automatically a parliamentary statute.
“Free and open Indo-Pacific” does not transfer national military command to the Quad.
memoryTip: “JIMEX joins Japan and India; Quad adds Australia and America.”

topic: Supreme Court and social justice law
category: sex selection, special statutory procedure, investigation and criminal cognisance
title: PC-PNDT Act Investigation and Cognisance
subtitle: The Supreme Court clarified the distinct roles of the Appropriate Authority, police and magistrate under a social-welfare penal statute, linking statutory interpretation, cognisance, investigation and protection against sex selection.
summary:
On 20 August 2026, the Supreme Court delivered its judgment in **State of Uttar Pradesh v. Brij Pal Singh**, 2026 INSC 901. It held that police cannot register an FIR and independently investigate offences created only by the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (PC-PNDT Act).

The Act assigns investigation to the statutory **Appropriate Authority**, and Section 28 permits a court to take cognisance only on a complaint by the Appropriate Authority, an authorised officer or an eligible person or organisation after statutory notice. A police chargesheet cannot become the foundation for cognisance of a PC-PNDT-only offence. Police may nevertheless investigate independent IPC or BNS offences and may provide supplementary operational assistance under the Appropriate Authority’s supervision.

keyMilestones.event: Parliament enacted the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act.
The central enactment came into force.
Parliament amended the law to cover pre-conception sex selection; the amended title became the PC-PNDT Act.
Rule 18A was inserted to standardise monitoring and enforcement, including the instruction to avoid police involvement as far as possible for PC-PNDT enforcement.
The Supreme Court granted leave in the appeal arising from prosecution in Uttar Pradesh.
In 2026 INSC 901, the Supreme Court clarified the exclusive statutory route for investigating PC-PNDT offences and taking cognisance.

keyArticles.desc: Special law controls its procedure governs When Parliament assigns investigation and prosecution to a designated authority, the general police process cannot override that special design.
Section 17(4) governs The Appropriate Authority investigates complaints, takes immediate action, searches and seizes records and pursues legal proceedings.
Rule 18A(3)(iv) governs Police involvement is to be avoided as far as possible for implementing the Act; police retain their ordinary role for independent offences under other laws.
Section 28 cognisance bar governs A court may take cognisance only on the specified statutory complaints. A police report is not one of them.
Two procedural tracks governs The same facts may disclose both PC-PNDT offences and separate IPC/BNS offences. The Appropriate Authority handles the former; police may investigate the latter.

Supplementary assistance governs Police can support the Appropriate Authority with security, tracing persons, digital or forensic help and preservation of evidence, without assuming statutory control.
Constitutional context governs The Act advances equality and dignity by combating sex selection and the systemic devaluation of girls, while criminal procedure remains governed by enacted safeguards.
Full form: PC-PNDT means Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection).
Purpose: Regulation of prenatal diagnostic techniques and prohibition of their misuse for sex selection or disclosure of fetal sex.
Article 14: Equality before law and equal protection of laws.
Article 15(1): Prohibits State discrimination on specified grounds including sex; Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children.
Article 21: Protects life and personal liberty, including dignity under constitutional jurisprudence.
Cognisance: The judicial act of taking notice of an alleged offence for proceeding according to law; it is distinct from investigation.
Special versus general law: A specific statutory procedure ordinarily prevails over a general procedure for the field it expressly occupies.

examTraps: The judgment did not legalise sex determination or weaken registration and record duties.
It did not prohibit police from investigating every offence arising from the same incident.
memoryTip: “17 investigates; 28 opens the court gate.”

topic: Supreme Court and social justice law
category: atrocities law, statutory ingredients, cognisance and quashing
title: SC/ST Act and the “Public View” Requirement
subtitle: The judgment offers a clean passage on statutory ingredients, “public view,” prima facie review at cognisance, anti-caste legislation and the difference between a public place and a place within public view.
summary:
On 20 August 2026, the Supreme Court delivered **Ramkrishna Chauhan v. State of Uttar Pradesh**, 2026 INSC 895. It quashed proceedings against a school manager under Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

The alleged incident occurred inside an enclosed school room with no window or public access. The FIR and witness statements did not attribute a specific caste-based utterance to the appellant or establish that a member of the public witnessed or heard it. The Court held that the statutory ingredient “in any place within public view” was not prima facie satisfied. Proceedings for the remaining IPC offences were allowed to continue.

keyMilestones.event: Parliament enacted the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
The Act came into force.
Parliament’s amendment expanded and reorganised the list of atrocities, including the present clauses (r) and (s).
In Hitesh Verma, the Supreme Court explained the “public view” ingredient in the context of alleged insult inside a building.
The FIR underlying Ramkrishna Chauhan was registered after a school dispute.
The Allahabad High Court declined to interfere with the summoning order.
The Supreme Court quashed only the SC/ST Act proceedings against the appellant while preserving the IPC proceedings.

keyArticles.desc: Essential ingredients governs Even at the prima facie stage, the FIR, chargesheet and supporting material must disclose the basic elements of the alleged statutory offence.

“Public view” governs Members of the public must be able to witness or hear the alleged utterance. A location does not qualify merely because it sits within a school or other premises generally associated with public activity.
Public place versus public view governs The statutory phrase focuses on visibility or audibility to the public, not simply ownership or classification of the location.
Specific allegation governs The Court also noted the absence of any specific caste-based words attributed to the appellant in the FIR or the complainant’s statement.
Limited quashing governs The ruling removed the SC/ST Act counts because their ingredients were absent; it did not adjudicate guilt on the surviving IPC allegations.

Constitutional setting governs Articles 17, 46, 338 and 338A reflect the constitutional commitment against untouchability and caste oppression. That objective coexists with the criminal-law requirement that every statutory ingredient be disclosed.
Article 17: Abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
Article 46: Directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially SCs and STs, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
Article 338: Provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.
Article 338A: Provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes.
Special Courts: The 1989 Act provides for Exclusive Special Courts or Special Courts for speedy trial.
Scheduled Castes and Tribes: Constitutional specification operates principally through Articles 341 and 342.

examTraps: A public institution is not automatically “within public view” in every interior room.
The judgment did not dilute the Act where all statutory ingredients are properly alleged.
memoryTip: “Public view asks who could see or hear.”

category: defined offences, penal statutes, Article 20(1) and gang-control legislation
title: UP Gangsters Act and the Principle of Legality
subtitle: The Supreme Court connected a state gang-control statute with Article 20(1), the maxim nullum crimen nulla poena sine lege, strict construction of penal laws and the distinction between defining a person and defining an offence.
summary:
On 20 August 2026, the Supreme Court delivered its judgment in **Shiv Pratap Singh alias Chinu v. State of Uttar Pradesh**, 2026 INSC 894. It quashed proceedings initiated against the appellants under Sections 2 and 3 of the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986.

The Court held that the Act defines a “gang” and a “gangster” but does not create a distinct substantive offence whose commission attracts the punishment in Section 3. A gang chart or earlier criminal case could not fill that legislative gap. The Court described the proceedings as legally unsustainable because criminal punishment requires a pre-existing, clearly defined offence. It expressly left the constitutional validity of the Act open and clarified that proceedings under other penal laws were unaffected.

keyMilestones.event: Uttar Pradesh enacted the Gangsters and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act.
The underlying criminal cases and gang charts relied upon against the appellants arose during this period.
The Allahabad High Court declined to interfere with the Gangsters Act proceedings challenged by the appellants.
The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and quashed the proceedings under Sections 2 and 3 of the Act.
Independent proceedings for offences under other penal enactments remain governed by those enactments; the Court did not invalidate the 1986 Act as a whole.

keyArticles.desc: Article 20(1) governs No person may be convicted except for violating a law in force at the time of the charged act, nor receive a greater penalty than the one then prescribed.

Principle of legality governs *Nullum crimen sine lege* means no crime without law; *nulla poena sine lege* means no punishment without law. The prohibited conduct and sanction must have a legislative basis.
Strict construction governs Penal statutes are construed strictly. Courts cannot cure the absence of an offence by implication, analogy or administrative practice.

Definition versus offence governs Defining “gang” and “gangster” identifies categories, but a criminal statute must also make specified conduct an offence. A status label is not by itself a complete actus reus.
Gang charts governs A gang chart may organise allegations or prior cases; it cannot substitute for the legislature’s duty to define criminal conduct.
Limited holding governs The Court quashed the proceedings before it. It did not rule on the Act’s overall constitutional validity and did not erase prosecutions under the IPC or other valid laws.
Article 20 protections: Article 20 contains protection against ex post facto criminal laws, double jeopardy and compelled self-incrimination.
Seventh Schedule: “Public order” and “police” are State List subjects, while criminal law and criminal procedure are principally in the Concurrent List, subject to constitutional distribution rules.
Actus reus and mens rea: Criminal responsibility ordinarily requires a prohibited act and the legally required mental element, though statutes may vary.
Rule of law: Citizens must be able to know in advance what conduct attracts criminal liability; executive discretion cannot replace enacted law.
Judicial review: Article 136 enables the Supreme Court, in its discretion, to grant special leave to appeal from judgments and orders of courts and tribunals.

examTraps: The Court did not hold that every gang-control law is unconstitutional.
Quashing Gangsters Act proceedings did not automatically quash valid charges under other laws.
memoryTip: “Define the deed before punishing the person.”

category: professional ethics, legal privilege, Advocates Act and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam
title: Advocate-Client Confidentiality and Professional Misconduct
subtitle: A Supreme Court ruling clarifies that an advocate's duty not to publicise confidential client information survives the end of the engagement and even an adversarial breakdown, while preserving the statutory crime-or-fraud exceptions.
summary:
On 21 August 2026, the Supreme Court in **Rehana Khan v. Rizwan Siddiquee, 2026 INSC 907** upheld the Bar Council of India's order suspending an advocate from practice for two years. The Court held that professional confidence does not disappear merely because the lawyer-client relationship ends or the former client and advocate become adversaries.

The advocate had disclosed alleged client communications through media interactions after a dispute. The Court distinguished lawful self-defence from public disclosure: a lawyer who is falsely accused may approach investigating authorities, produce material in a proper legal proceeding and pursue remedies such as defamation, but cannot use television or other public platforms to reveal privileged or confidential communications. It dismissed cross-appeals by both sides and, because of their conduct in the litigation, directed each side to pay ₹5 lakh to the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee.

keyMilestones.event: Parliament enacts the Advocates Act, creating the statutory disciplinary framework for advocates and Bar Councils.
The Bar Council of India Rules codify standards of professional conduct and etiquette, including duties owed to clients.
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaces the Indian Evidence Act; Section 132 carries forward the rule on professional communications.
The Bar Council of India finds professional misconduct and imposes a two-year suspension.
The Supreme Court dismisses both sides' appeals and affirms that confidentiality survives termination and hostility between lawyer and former client.

memoryTip: **132 stays after you** — Section 132 survives the end of the lawyer-client relationship.

category: judicial service, entry-level recruitment, court training and Article 234
title: Civil Judge Recruitment and the One-Year Practice Rule
subtitle: The Supreme Court replaced the restored three-year practice condition for entry-level judicial service with a phased one-year rule and a compulsory training-plus-clerkship structure, linking a current judgment to Articles 233-237 and the history of judicial-service reform.
summary:
On 21 August 2026, a three-judge Bench of the Supreme Court in **Bhumika Trust v. Union of India, 2026 INSC 904** modified the entry conditions for recruitment as Civil Judge (Junior Division). The majority, speaking through Chief Justice Surya Kant with Justice Augustine George Masih, reduced the minimum pre-recruitment practice requirement from three years to one year and created a transition regime. Justice K. Vinod Chandran dissented.

For recruitment processes notified between 20 May 2025 and 31 March 2027, eligible law graduates may apply without producing a practice certificate. A selected candidate is to be treated as a trainee judicial officer and must complete one year at the State Judicial Academy followed by a structured one-year clerkship: six months with the District/Higher Judiciary and six months with a sitting High Court judge. For recruitment notifications issued on or after 1 April 2027, a candidate must first complete one year of actual practice before undergoing the same training and clerkship. The Court directed State Governments and High Courts to amend their rules within three months and said the scheme may be reviewed after five years.

keyMilestones.event: The Supreme Court in the first All India Judges' Association decision supports three years' practice for entry-level judicial appointments.
The Court removes the practice requirement following the Shetty Commission process, allowing fresh law graduates to compete.
The Supreme Court prospectively restores a three-year minimum practice condition.
The 2026 judgment treats this as the transition window; applicants need no practice certificate but selected candidates must complete the two-stage training structure.
Bhumika Trust v. Union of India reduces the future pre-entry requirement to one year by a 2:1 majority.
New recruitment notifications must require one year of actual practice, followed by one year at a Judicial Academy and one year of structured clerkship.
State Governments and High Courts are expected to align their recruitment rules within the Court's three-month period.

memoryTip: **1-1-1 after 2027** — one practice year, one academy year, one clerkship year.

category: electronics manufacturing, production incentives, domestic value addition and supply chains
title: Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme
subtitle: The notified ₹62,500 crore scheme succeeds the large-scale electronics PLI and connects industrial policy, domestic brands, value addition, fiscal incentives and global supply-chain strategy.
summary:
On 21 August 2026, the Union Government notified the **Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme (MPMS)**, following Cabinet approval on 15 July 2026. The five-year scheme runs from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31 with a total outlay of **₹62,500 crore**. It succeeds the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for Large Scale Electronics Manufacturing, whose scheduled period ended on 31 March 2026.

MPMS offers incentives linked to incremental eligible sales. The approved structure provides a base incentive ranging from **2.25% to 5%**, an additional incentive of up to **1.5%** for domestic sourcing of specified components, and an additional **3%** for eligible Indian-brand expenditure on design and research and development. The Government projects production of about **₹39 lakh crore** over five years and around **60,000 direct jobs**. These are policy targets, not guaranteed outcomes.

keyMilestones.event: The Union Government notifies the PLI Scheme for Large Scale Electronics Manufacturing.
The PLI period supports expansion in mobile-phone production and exports.
The scheduled large-scale electronics PLI period ends.
The Union Cabinet approves MPMS with a ₹62,500 crore outlay.
The Government notifies the scheme for operation from FY 2026-27.
Final financial year of the five-year MPMS period.

memoryTip: **Phone 5-39-60** — five years, ₹39 lakh crore projected production, 60,000 projected direct jobs.

category: Biological Diversity Act, genetic resources, local benefit claimers and Nagoya Protocol
title: Biodiversity Access and Benefit-Sharing
subtitle: The National Biodiversity Authority's in-window disbursal gives a concrete application of Section 21 of the Biological Diversity Act and connects genetic resources, federal institutions, community rights, the CBD, Nagoya Protocol and global biodiversity targets.
summary:
On 22 August 2026, the National Biodiversity Authority announced the disbursal of **₹2.82 crore** under India's access and benefit-sharing (ABS) mechanism. Of this, **₹2.80 crore** was released to 27 State Biodiversity Boards and three Union Territory Biodiversity Councils. The underlying payment came from Advanta Enterprises Limited, formerly UPL Limited, for use of genetic resources associated with 24 hybrids: eight cauliflower, five hot-pepper, five okra and six tomato hybrids.

Because the specific places from which the biological resources were accessed and the individual benefit claimers could not be identified, the amount was distributed among the State and Union Territory institutions on the basis described by the Authority. A further **₹2.01 lakh** was released to ICAR-Indian Institute of Horticultural Research, Karnataka, in relation to two microbial strains used by Sumitomo Chemical India Limited. The release said total ABS disbursals had crossed **₹185 crore**.

keyMilestones.event: The Convention on Biological Diversity is opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit.
Parliament enacts the Biological Diversity Act.
The National Biodiversity Authority is established in Chennai.
The Nagoya Protocol on ABS is adopted in Nagoya, Japan.
The Nagoya Protocol enters into force internationally.
India issues national ABS guidelines under the Biological Diversity Act.
The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 comes into force.
Updated Biological Diversity Rules and ABS Regulations take effect.
NBA announces the ₹2.82 crore disbursal and reports cumulative releases above ₹185 crore.

keyArticles.desc: Section 21, Biological Diversity Act governs Requires the NBA, while granting relevant approval, to secure fair and equitable sharing of benefits on mutually agreed terms between the applicant and the BMC represented by the NBA.

Federal and local design governs NBA, SBBs and BMCs distribute authority across national, State and local institutions. A People’s Biodiversity Register records local biological resources and knowledge but does not itself transfer ownership of every recorded item.

memoryTip: **Access, Agree, Allocate** — lawful access, mutually agreed terms, fair allocation.

category: Disaster cooperation, shared rivers and neighbourhood diplomacy
title: India–Nepal Relations
subtitle: The August 2026 flash-flood response connects India–Nepal relations with shared Himalayan river systems, disaster management, federal coordination, consular protection and humanitarian assistance.
summary: On 26 August 2026, a destructive flash flood in northern Nepal prompted a coordinated Indian response. The Union Home Ministry said the Centre was monitoring the situation with the Ministries of External Affairs, Jal Shakti and Defence; the Home Minister spoke with the Chief Ministers of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh; administrations and rescue teams, including the NDRF, were placed on alert in potentially affected Indian border areas; and the Embassy of India in Kathmandu issued emergency contacts for Indian nationals. Independent reporting confirmed downstream alerts in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and India's readiness to assist Nepal. The cause and casualty totals were still evolving at the verification cutoff, so this dossier records the settled governmental response rather than provisional figures.

keyMilestones.event: India and Nepal signed the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, a foundational instrument in their modern bilateral relationship.
Parliament enacted the Disaster Management Act, providing India's institutional framework for disaster management.
India and Nepal established a three-tier bilateral mechanism for water resources and flood-management issues.
India's MEA annual report recorded the Joint Committee on Inundation and Flood Management as a forum for bilateral flood and inundation discussions.
The Nepal flash flood triggered downstream alerts and inter-ministerial monitoring in India.
Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were advised to remain alert; rescue teams and the NDRF were placed on standby in vulnerable border areas.
The Embassy of India in Kathmandu activated emergency contacts for affected Indian nationals, while India indicated readiness to assist Nepal.

keyArticles.desc: Article 51(c) of the Constitution governs Directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.
Article 253 of the Constitution governs Empowers Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, agreements and international decisions.
Union List Entry 10 governs Places foreign affairs and relations with foreign countries within Parliament's domain.
Union List Entry 14 governs Covers entering into treaties and agreements and implementing them.
State List Entries 17 and 18 governs Cover water, irrigation, canals and land, subject to constitutional limits including Union power over inter-State rivers.
Article 262 and Union List Entry 56 governs Concern adjudication and regulation of inter-State rivers within India; they are not, by themselves, a treaty framework for a river shared with Nepal.
Disaster Management Act, 2005 governs Establishes national, state and district disaster-management authorities and provides for coordinated response measures.
Consular protection governs The Embassy's assistance facilitates communication and evacuation but does not displace Nepal's territorial jurisdiction.
Nepal: A landlocked Himalayan country; its capital is Kathmandu.
Open border: Indian and Nepali citizens have a distinctive mobility relationship shaped by bilateral practice and the 1950 treaty.
Gandak system: The Gandak, known upstream as the Narayani, carries Himalayan waters from Nepal into Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
Kosi system: Another major transboundary river system linking Nepal's catchments with Bihar.
NDRF: A specialised force constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
Central Water Commission: A technical organisation under the Union Ministry of Jal Shakti dealing with water resources, including flood forecasting.
Non-refoulement is unrelated here: Consular evacuation after a disaster must not be confused with refugee-law protection against forced return.

examTraps: Do not use provisional casualty totals or present an unsettled cause as established.
Do not confuse assistance to Nepal with a unilateral right to operate inside Nepal.
Do not treat Article 262 as the constitutional basis for every international river arrangement.
memoryTip: “River, Response, Relations: CWC, NDRF, Embassy.”

category: Human-rights treaties, equality and treaty-body monitoring
title: India’s ICERD Review and CERD Concluding Observations
subtitle: India's first CERD dialogue since 2007 connects a UN human-rights treaty with Articles 14-17, caste and descent, citizenship, refugee protection, electoral rolls, treaty monitoring and the legal status of non-binding recommendations.
summary: On 25 August 2026, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination closed its 118th session after adopting concluding observations on India under the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD). The review covered India's combined twentieth and twenty-first periodic reports and followed a public dialogue on 11-12 August—India's first such dialogue since 2007. The Committee recorded concerns and recommendations concerning discrimination, alleged law-enforcement abuses, hate speech, treatment of Rohingya and Bengali-speaking Muslims, the Assam National Register of Citizens and reported effects of electoral-roll revision. On 26 August, India rejected what it described as politically motivated and malicious references, disputed sweeping generalisations and an expanded reading of the Convention's mandate, reaffirmed its constitutional safeguards and said it would respond through the established procedure. The Committee's observations are authoritative treaty-monitoring recommendations, not a judgment of an international court.

category: Export controls, defence manufacturing and strategic trade
title: Defence Export OGEL and SCOMET Reforms
subtitle: The 2026 defence-export reforms link the Foreign Trade framework, SCOMET controls, UN arms embargoes, end-use safeguards, India’s Wassenaar Arrangement membership and the balance between ease of business and national-security regulation.
summary: On 28 August 2026, the Department of Defence Production announced a revised Defence Export Standard Operating Procedure and a unified Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework. Three existing OGEL procedures—for major platforms and equipment, parts and components, and intra-company transfer of technology—were consolidated. Standard validity increased from two to three years, and geographic coverage expanded from 41 countries to all destinations except negative or sensitive countries and those subject to United Nations Security Council sanctions or arms embargoes. The reforms also removed routine stakeholder consultation for most non-lethal exports and for items sent to international tenders or exhibitions, created a route linked to long-term contracts with foreign original equipment manufacturers and broadened eligible items. The change reduces repeat paperwork; it does not authorise unrestricted export of every weapon, technology or destination.

The Wassenaar Arrangement began operation.

India reported defence production of ₹1.78 lakh crore and defence exports of ₹38,424 crore.

category: India–US defence cooperation, arms transfers and military modernisation
title: India–US Javelin Missile Acquisition and Foreign Military Sales
subtitle: The signed Javelin Letter of Offer and Acceptance connects India–US strategic relations with the government-to-government Foreign Military Sales process, legislative oversight of public expenditure, arms-transfer controls, indigenous defence production and the distinction between a notified ceiling and final contract terms.
summary: On 28 August 2026, the Indian Army signed a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA) to acquire the Javelin anti-tank guided missile system through the United States Foreign Military Sales (FMS) process. The U.S. Mission in India described the LOA as a government-to-government agreement and said that it could lead to future industrial collaboration. The current official announcement did not disclose the final price, quantity or delivery schedule. A November 2025 U.S. congressional notification had described a *possible* package of 100 Javelin rounds, one fly-to-buy missile, 25 command launch units and support at a maximum estimated value of US$45.7 million. That earlier ceiling is useful background but is not proof of the final 2026 contract terms. Co-production also remains a possibility for future discussion, not a term established by the public announcement.

title: Article 12 “State” and Article 131 Original Jurisdiction
subtitle: The Supreme Court drew an exam-ready distinction between the enlarged definition of “State” in Article 12 and the constituent States that alone can invoke Article 131.
summary:
In Lucknow Development Authority v. Union of India, 2026 INSC 923, the Supreme Court held that a statutory authority cannot invoke the Court's original jurisdiction under Article 131. The Allahabad High Court had dismissed a long-pending writ petition by the Lucknow Development Authority (LDA), reasoning that the land dispute involved the Union and a State and should be taken directly to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court set that order aside and remitted the writ petition to the High Court for an expeditious merits decision.

The Court stressed that LDA may fall within the broad expression “the State” in Article 12 for fundamental-rights scrutiny, but it is not a constituent “State” named in the First Schedule. Article 131 uses the latter, narrower meaning. The judgment was delivered on 21 August 2026 and published on the Supreme Court's latest-judgments page on 29 August 2026.

keyMilestones.event: Uttar Pradesh enacted the law under which LDA was constituted.
LDA instituted the writ proceedings that later remained pending for roughly twenty-five years.
The Allahabad High Court dismissed the petition with liberty to invoke Article 131.
The Supreme Court allowed LDA's appeal and restored the writ petition.
Reportable judgment 2026 INSC 923 appeared on the Supreme Court's latest-judgments page.

examTraps: Do not say the Court resolved title or that all Article 12 bodies can sue under Article 131.
memoryTip: “12 tests authorities; 131 settles federation parties.”

title: Bona Fide Land-Title Disputes and Limits on Summary Eviction
subtitle: The Supreme Court reaffirmed that the executive cannot decide a genuine, long-standing title dispute through summary eviction proceedings and must seek adjudication by a competent court.
summary:
In M/s Circar Paper Mills Ltd. v. District Collector, Nellore District, 2026 INSC 924, the Supreme Court held that the State could not use summary proceedings to evict occupants where ownership was genuinely disputed. The State claimed land associated with a paper mill was government-assigned land; the competing private claim relied on a decades-long chain of registered transactions, revenue entries, industrial possession, liquidation proceedings, and a court-supervised auction.

The Court restored the Company Judge's auction order and the purchaser's possession, while reviving connected writ proceedings so rival claims could be adjudicated in the proper forum. It applied Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Thummala Krishna Rao, which says summary eviction is unsuitable for bona fide title disputes. The judgment was delivered on 25 August and published on 29 August 2026.

keyMilestones.event: Documents relied on by private parties began the asserted title and possession chain.
Circar Paper Mills purchased land and operated an industrial unit.
The Official Liquidator took possession during winding-up proceedings.
The Company Court approved the auction and sale.
Proceedings that ultimately reached the Supreme Court were instituted.
The Supreme Court delivered 2026 INSC 924.
The judgment appeared on the latest-judgments page.

examTraps: Neither long possession nor a judicial auction was declared an automatic source of indefeasible title.
memoryTip: “Real title fight? Summary route is not right.”

category: Central Asia, strategic partnerships, trade, connectivity and executive agreements
title: India–Uzbekistan Comprehensive Strategic Partnership
subtitle: The 2026 partnership upgrade links India's Central Asia policy, executive agreements, trade and connectivity, critical minerals, digital payments, multilateral institutions and the constitutional distribution of foreign-affairs powers.
summary:
On 30 August 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev elevated India–Uzbekistan relations from a **Strategic Partnership** to a **Comprehensive Strategic Partnership** during talks in Tashkent. The two sides set a target of raising bilateral trade to **US$5 billion by 2030**, agreed to create a Foreign Ministers-led implementation mechanism and decided to upgrade their Intergovernmental Commission to the ministerial level.

The official outcomes list records **11 MoUs, agreements and cooperation programmes**. They cover culture, conservation of the Buddhist sites of Fayaz Tepa and Kara Tepa, archives, Ayurveda and traditional medicine, geology and mineral resources, tourism, diplomatic training, economic and financial dialogue, environmental protection, higher education and scientific research, and a Gujarat–Samarkand regional partnership.

Five further announcements included a **US$1 million grant** for ecological rehabilitation in the Aral Sea region, 100 Lal Bahadur Shastri Hindi scholarships, an ICCR Sanskrit Chair in Tashkent and a commercial arrangement enabling Indian UPI apps to scan Uzbekistan's UZQR merchant-payment codes. The package is a completed diplomatic outcome, but it is not a military alliance, a concluded preferential trade agreement or a transfer of legislative power to either government.

keyMilestones.event: India and Uzbekistan established diplomatic relations.
The two countries declared a Strategic Partnership.
India announced its Connect Central Asia policy.
Narendra Modi made a bilateral visit to Uzbekistan during a tour of all five Central Asian republics.
India hosted the first India–Central Asia Summit in virtual format.
The latest edition of the bilateral military exercise Dustlik was held in Uzbekistan's Namangan Region.
Modi paid a State Visit to Uzbekistan.
The leaders elevated ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, issued a joint statement and announced the cooperation package.
The two governments aim to raise bilateral trade to US$5 billion; this is a target, not a guaranteed result.

keyArticles.desc: Article 73 of the Constitution governs The Union executive power extends to matters on which Parliament may legislate and to rights exercisable by the Government of India under a treaty or agreement, subject to constitutional limits.
Article 253 governs Parliament may enact laws to implement treaties, agreements, conventions and international decisions, including beyond the ordinary federal distribution of subjects.
Union List governs Foreign affairs, diplomatic representation, treaties and agreements, defence and participation in international organisations fall within Union competence.
Article 51(c) governs A Directive Principle asks the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.

MoUs and agreements governs Their precise legal effect depends on their text, intent and any domestic implementation required. The outcomes list alone does not prove that every instrument is a treaty requiring the same form of implementation.

No concluded trade pact governs The leaders directed ministries to explore next steps after a joint feasibility study on a preferential trade agreement. That direction is not itself a PTA or tariff concession.
No collective-defence clause governs Security cooperation, intelligence sharing and Exercise Dustlik do not create a NATO-style obligation to enter a war for the other party.

Capital of Uzbekistan: Tashkent.
Uzbekistan's neighbours: Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan.

Dustlik: India–Uzbekistan joint military exercise; “Dustlik” means friendship.

category: cooperative federalism, inter-State rivers, Bihar Reorganisation Act and water governance
title: Bihar–Jharkhand Sone River Water Agreement
subtitle: The 31 August 2026 agreement ended a 25-year allocation dispute and links Article 262, Parliament's river-dispute law, the Bihar Reorganisation Act, zonal councils, basin geography and cooperative federalism.
summary:
On 31 August 2026, Bihar and Jharkhand signed a memorandum of understanding in New Delhi to settle their long-running dispute over the share of Sone River water inherited from undivided Bihar. The agreement was signed in the presence of Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren and Union Jal Shakti Minister C. R. Patil. The Union government described it as ending a 25-year dispute and enabling irrigation, drinking-water and regional development benefits.

Independent reports state that undivided Bihar's 7.75 million acre-feet allocation under the 1973 Bansagar Agreement is now divided as 5.75 MAF for Bihar and 2.00 MAF for Jharkhand. The official press release confirms the settlement and signing but does not reproduce the full MoU text or those detailed allocation clauses; the figures should therefore be attributed to the corroborating reports unless the MoU is later published.

keyMilestones.event: Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and undivided Bihar concluded the Bansagar Agreement for sharing Sone waters.
Jharkhand was created under the Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000, creating the need to divide undivided Bihar's water share and project interests.
Bihar submitted a preliminary project report for the Indrapuri reservoir project to the Central Water Commission.
The Central Water Commission returned the report pending resolution of the allocation and co-basin State no-objection issues.
The dispute was discussed at the Standing Committee of the Eastern Zonal Council.
Bihar and Jharkhand signed the MoU in New Delhi; the Union government announced that the 25-year dispute had been settled.

keyArticles.desc: Article 262 governs Parliament may provide for adjudication of disputes over an inter-State river or river valley and may exclude court jurisdiction in such disputes.

Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 governs Provides the statutory tribunal route when negotiation fails and the statutory conditions are met. This MoU is a negotiated settlement, not a tribunal award.

Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000 governs Sections 78–82 address rights, liabilities and arrangements concerning water-resource projects after reorganisation, including Union directions and possible management structures.
Entry 17, State List governs Water, irrigation and canals are ordinarily State subjects, subject to Entry 56 of the Union List.
Entry 56, Union List governs Parliament may regulate and develop inter-State rivers and river valleys to the extent declared expedient in the public interest.

Cooperative federalism governs The settlement illustrates executive negotiation among States with Union facilitation. It does not amend Article 262 or replace the statutory tribunal system for other disputes.
Agreement versus adjudication governs A consensual MoU draws authority from agreement and applicable statutes; it is legally distinct from a judicial judgment or an inter-State river tribunal award.
Sone River: Rises near the Amarkantak plateau and flows north-east through central and eastern India before joining the Ganga near Patna.
River classification: The Sone is a right-bank tributary of the Ganga.
Bansagar Dam: Built on the Sone in Madhya Pradesh and named after the Sanskrit scholar Bana Bhatt.
Successor States: Jharkhand became India's 28th State on 15 November 2000.
Zonal Councils: Statutory bodies established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; the Union Home Minister is their common Chairperson.
MAF: One million acre-feet is a volume measure equal to about 1.233 billion cubic metres.

category: CPC Sections 13 and 44A, execution, corporate veil and contempt
title: Foreign Decrees, Asset Security and Contempt Undertakings
subtitle: The Supreme Court linked foreign-decree execution under Section 44A CPC with comity, asset-preservation orders, corporate separateness and the strict test for treating a statement as a contempt undertaking.
summary:
On 1 September 2026, the Supreme Court decided **Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority v. Matrix Pharmacorp Private Limited**, 2026 INSC 932. The litigation arose from efforts by Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority (RAKIA) to execute in India a decree obtained in the United Arab Emirates.

The Court upheld the finding that a statement in a counter-affidavit—recording that a company had then decided not to make an acquisition—was not an unconditional undertaking whose breach would support contempt. At the same time, it directed the respondents jointly and severally to provide an additional **₹200 crore security** within two weeks. It left the issues of a unified family-controlled structure and lifting the corporate veil to the executing Commercial Courts at Hyderabad and Ranga Reddy, which were directed to decide the execution proceedings within four months.
memoryTip: Focus recall on key legal terms.

category: Finance Act 1979, delayed remittance, administrative discretion and fair appellate procedure
title: Foreign Travel Tax Penalty and No Reformatio in Peius
subtitle: The Supreme Court distinguished failure to pay tax from delayed remittance, rejected automatic penalty and applied no reformatio in peius as a principle of fair procedure and natural justice.
summary:
On 1 September 2026, the Supreme Court decided **M/s Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India**, 2026 INSC 933. The airline had collected the now-discontinued Foreign Travel Tax (FTT) but deposited it late on six occasions. Authorities treated the delay as failure to pay under Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979 and ultimately increased an original ₹12,000 penalty to ₹71,29,140 after remand.

The Court held that delayed deposit fell under **Section 38(4)** read with Rules 4 and 9 of the Foreign Travel Tax Rules, 1979, not Section 38(3). Penalty was discretionary rather than automatic, and the authorities had overlooked explanations that could support condonation. It set aside the penalty, ordered refund of any amount paid with **9% annual interest within three months**, and discharged the bank guarantee.

category: Eurasian security, regional institutions and the Bishkek Declaration
title: SCO Summit
subtitle: The 26th SCO summit combined terrorism, regional connectivity, Afghanistan, institutional reform and India-led initiatives in a high-yield international-organisation setting.
summary:
The **26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Council of Heads of State** met in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, from 31 August to 1 September 2026, during the SCO's twenty-fifth anniversary year. Leaders adopted the **Bishkek Declaration**, four memoranda of understanding and more than twenty decisions and statements.

India identified thirteen principal outcomes, including an SCO Universal Centre for Countering Security Threats, anti-narcotics cooperation to 2030, and cooperation on energy, disaster management, artificial intelligence, climate, nuclear safety and information. Prime Minister Narendra Modi framed India's approach through **Security, Connectivity and Opportunity**, opposed double standards on terrorism, and said connectivity must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity. India also proposed English as an official language under the SCO Charter and advanced forums for civilisational dialogue, young scientists and young authors.

The SCO was established in Shanghai with Uzbekistan as the sixth founding member.
The Charter was signed, entered into force, and the Secretariat and RATS became operational.
India and Pakistan joined as full members.
Iran and then Belarus became full members.
The 26th Council of Heads of State adopted the Bishkek Declaration and an institutional package.
